Definition: Whether the instant payment system is used or can be used for government disbursements to citizens, including social transfers, welfare payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies, grants, and emergency assistance.
Comments: Evidence of digitized government-to-person style use (social transfers/benefit disbursements) not found as active nationwide; older ecosystem research indicates P2G initiatives and some public-service payments, but not definitive active G2P scale in this step.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light-touch search surfaced multiple authoritative sources (World Bank, official LODA government site, AfricaNenda SIIPS), so the row was escalated to full verification rather than confirmed as Unknown. Evidence shows active digital disbursement for specific G2P programmes (pensions, and VUP cash transfers via a 2025 mobile-money rollout), but the national instant payment system (eKash) itself did not yet carry G2P transactions as of the 2023 AfricaNenda case study, which listed social transfers as a later phase of roll-out. Recalculated from 0 to 2 (Limited Use) rather than 3 (Active Use via the instant payment system specifically).
revised_comments: The Government of Rwanda disburses a range of government-to-person payments digitally, including old-age and civil-service pensions through the RSSB/Ejo Heza scheme, which has been fully digitised since 2022 and paid into individual bank accounts, and Vision Umurenge Programme (VUP) cash transfers, which the Local Administrative Entities Development Agency (LODA) is transitioning from semi-digitised SACCO-based payouts to direct mobile-phone disbursement. The 'My Phone, My Money' campaign, launched in August 2025 in Burera, Nyamagabe and Rusizi districts, links VUP beneficiaries' SACCO accounts to registered SIM cards so that support can be withdrawn via MTN or Airtel mobile money agents, with roll-out continuing district by district. The national instant payment system, eKash, does not yet itself carry G2P transactions; as of 2023 it supported only person-to-person payments, with bulk disbursements and social transfers listed as later phases of roll-out. Digital G2P use is therefore active for specific programmes disbursed through banks, SACCOs and mobile money, but is not yet comprehensive or routed through the interoperable instant payment system.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: Searched for explicit pro-poor governance mechanisms (e.g., consumer/low-income representation in scheme governance; inclusion mandates embedded in governance structures) for eKash/RNDPS/RSwitch and NBR payments governance, but only found general inclusion intent (cashless/inclusion strategy statements) without identified governance mechanisms.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light-touch search surfaced the Prime Minister's Order establishing the National Payment Council (a primary legal instrument) and the AfricaNenda SIIPS 2023 case study describing eKash's board composition, so the row was escalated to full verification. These sources show some inclusion mechanisms (civil-society board seat, consumer protection regulation) but no explicit reserved seat or mandate for vulnerable/low-income representation, so the score was recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial) rather than confirmed as Unknown or scored as 'Yes'.
revised_comments: Rwanda's payment system governance combines a regulator-led National Payment Council, chaired by the National Bank of Rwanda and including seats for the Bankers' Association, the Association of Microfinance Institutions, the Capital Market Authority, the Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority, and rotating mobile-money and payment-operator representatives, with the eKash instant payment system's own participant-owned board, which since 2023 has included a civil-society representative alongside banking, mobile-money and fintech members. Consumers of payment services are further protected under National Bank of Rwanda Regulation N°31/2019 on Protection of Payment Service Users and the Financial Service Consumer Protection Act (2021), and the sector-wide National Financial Inclusion Strategy 2019–2024 sets inclusion objectives that the payment system strategy is expected to support. There is, however, no dedicated consumer advisory board, reserved seat for small or non-bank payment service providers, or explicit pro-poor/vulnerable-population mandate written into the payment system's own governance charter, so representation of low-income users' interests remains indirect rather than structurally guaranteed.

IMF FAS data give 802.8 active mobile money accounts per 1,000 adults in 2024 (approximately 80%), corroborated by FinScope 2024 and the National Bank of Rwanda's inclusion roadmap. revised_comments: IMF Financial Access Survey data show 802.8 active mobile money accounts per 1,000 adults in Rwanda in 2024, equivalent to roughly 80% of the adult population holding an actively used mobile money account. This is corroborated by the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda's FinScope 2024 survey and the National Bank of Rwanda's National Financial Inclusion Roadmap 2026–2030, which record that around 69.5% of adults (5.95 million people) used mobile money and that mobile money usage rose from 34% of adults in 2016 to 77% in 2024, with daily and weekly usage also increasing markedly over the same period. Taken together, these sources place the share of adults actively transacting digitally within the 70–89% band.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: No credible evidence found for payment-system accessibility provisions for persons with disabilities in Rwanda (searched for disability access requirements for eKash/RNDPS/mobile money and national payment policies).
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light-touch search surfaced the FinScope 2024 Thematic Report on Financial Inclusion for Persons with Disabilities (Access to Finance Rwanda / National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda), so the row was escalated to full verification. The report and a February 2026 policy dialogue document persistent accessibility barriers and call for accessibility standards to be developed, with no evidence found of existing formal accessibility features in payment systems. Recalculated from 0 to 1 (No).
revised_comments: Rwanda's FinScope 2024 Thematic Report on Financial Inclusion for Persons with Disabilities finds that people with disabilities are markedly less included in digital and formal financial services than the rest of the adult population: mobile money account ownership among persons with disabilities is around 45-46%, against 59% for adults without disabilities, and formal saving among persons with disabilities has fallen from 47.7% in 2020 to 36.5% in 2024. Access to Finance Rwanda, the Mastercard Foundation and the National Union of Disability Organisations of Rwanda (NUDOR) held a policy dialogue in February 2026 highlighting persisting supply-side barriers, including physical inaccessibility of financial institution and mobile network operator premises, a lack of disability-tailored products, and gaps in accessible communication, and called for accessibility standards and inclusive product design to be developed. No evidence was found of payment service providers having implemented formal accessibility features (such as screen-reader compatibility, audio interfaces or accessible agent protocols) or of a disability-inclusion policy specific to digital payments, indicating that accessibility provision for persons with disabilities remains largely absent.

Definition: Percentage of government payments (G2P disbursements including salaries, pensions, social transfers) made through instant digital payment system rather than cash or check, reflecting government adoption and modernization.
Comments: No credible quantified evidence found for the share of government payments digitized in Rwanda (searched for World Bank G2P stats, national reporting, and program dashboards; found qualitative statements but no percentage covering government payments overall).
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light-touch search surfaced substantial but conflicting evidence on the share of government-to-person payments made digitally, so the row was escalated to full verification. Evidence indicates civil-service pension contributions and benefit records (RSSB/Ejo Heza) have been fully digitised since 2022 and civil-service payroll is processed through the IFMIS treasury system, but the largest social safety-net programme (VUP cash transfers) was, as of the World Bank's 2023 G2P workshop documentation, still 'semi-digitised' for most beneficiaries, and LODA's 'My Phone, My Money' mobile disbursement campaign had only reached 3 of Rwanda's 30 districts as of August 2025, with national roll-out ongoing. No single authoritative source gives an aggregate percentage of all government payments (by value or volume) made digitally, so the correct band on the 5-point scale cannot be determined with confidence from the sources reviewed. Left unscored and flagged for human review; a specific G2P payment digitisation statistic (e.g. from an IMF/World Bank G2P dataset or a Rwandan treasury report) would be needed to score this reliably.
revised_comments: Rwanda has digitised several major categories of government-to-person payment, including old-age and civil-service pension contributions and benefits managed by the Rwanda Social Security Board, which have been fully digital and disbursed to bank accounts since 2022, and civil-service salaries processed through the integrated financial management information system. The government's flagship social safety-net programme, the Vision Umurenge Programme, has historically relied on a semi-digitised process in which beneficiaries collect cash in person from Umurenge SACCOs, and the Local Administrative Entities Development Agency is now rolling out direct mobile-money disbursement, beginning in three districts in August 2025 and expanding nationwide. The overall share of government payments made digitally therefore varies considerably by programme and continues to increase, but no consolidated national figure covering all government-to-person payment types is currently published.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No credible evidence found for specific refugee/migrant access provisions (e.g., KYC exceptions, UNHCR mobile money programs in Rwanda tied to national payment rails) in this step.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A single light-touch search surfaced multiple authoritative sources (Alliance for Financial Inclusion, UNHCR-linked studies via RFILC and ReliefWeb), so the row was escalated to full verification. These document real but incomplete legal access for refugees and asylum-seekers, so the score was recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial).
revised_comments: Recognised refugees in Rwanda have legal access to formal financial services: under Directive N°01/FIU/2018 of the Financial Investigation Unit on anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism, a refugee ID card is an accepted identity document for bank account KYC/CDD purposes, and refugees are eligible for SIM card registration, which by default activates a mobile money wallet. Camp-based refugees also receive cash assistance through mobile money, notably MTN Mobile Money, and through Equity Bank accounts linked to UNHCR and World Food Programme cash-transfer programmes. Asylum-seekers, treated as non-residents, initially faced more restrictive documentary requirements, but an August 2021 directive from the Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority extended SIM, and therefore mobile money, registration to asylum-seekers using any legal document used to enter the country, including proof-of-registration documents issued by UNHCR and the Ministry in Charge of Emergency Management. Practical barriers persist, including limited national validation of refugee identity documents by some financial institutions and continued reliance on case-by-case regulatory approvals rather than explicit statutory recognition of refugee status in electronic-money regulations, meaning access, while real, remains only partial rather than fully equivalent to that of nationals.
